opus-5.5.text:
Cognitive science has been a big influence, more than people might think. I've talked many times about a chart my colleague Emmanuel Dupoux put together, showing roughly the age at which infants acquire various concepts about the world. Babies learn that objects are permanent, that unsupported objects fall, that solid objects don't pass through each other, notions of inertia and gravity, all in the first several months of life. Almost all of that is learned by observation, not language and not much interaction. A baby at four months can barely act on the world, yet it is building a model of how the world works.

That tells you two things. First, most of what we know isn't linguistic. It's this kind of intuitive physics and common sense, the stuff we never write down because it's obvious. That's why I keep saying that training on text alone will never get us to human-level intelligence. A four-year-old has seen about as much data through vision as the biggest LLMs have seen in text, and it's much richer, high-bandwidth, continuous data.

Second, babies don't learn this by predicting every pixel of what they'll see next. The world is full of unpredictable details: the exact texture of the carpet, how leaves move in the wind. If you train a system to reconstruct all of that, it wastes its capacity on noise. What a child seems to do is learn abstract representations and make predictions at that level: the ball will fall, the person will come back. That's essentially the motivation for joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA. You predict in representation space, not input space, so the system can discard what's unpredictable and keep what's relevant.

There's also the distinction psychologists make, popularized by Kahneman, between System 1 and System 2. System 1 is fast, reactive, intuitive. System 2 is deliberate: you imagine the consequences of your actions and plan. Current LLMs are basically System 1. They produce one token after another without really reasoning or planning. A world model is what makes System 2 possible: you have a model that predicts the next state of the world given an action, and you search for a sequence of actions that optimizes some objective, subject to guardrails. That's how I think about objective-driven AI.

And animals are a good reminder too. A cat has a remarkably good model of the physical world. It can plan complex jumps, it understands its environment, and it does all that without any language. We don't yet have AI systems as smart as a cat in that sense. So cognitive science, and observing animals and children, keeps reminding us what's missing, and points to the kind of architecture we need to build.

r001.rationale: It describes System 2 as imagining the consequences of actions and planning a sequence of actions.

r002.rationale: It connects cognitive-science observations to JEPA and world models, but does not identify a substantial gap between that inspiration and its translation into a neural architecture.

r003.rationale: It says predicting every pixel or reconstructing unpredictable details wastes capacity, and favors predicting in representation space instead.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, cognitive science has been enormously influential, probably more than most people realize. The whole idea that an intelligent system needs an internal model of the world, that it should predict the consequences of its actions before taking them, that comes straight out of cognitive science and developmental psychology.

Look at what people like Emmanuel Dupoux have shown about infants. A baby learns intuitive physics, that objects persist when they're hidden, that unsupported things fall, that solid objects don't pass through each other, in the first few months of life. Nobody tells the baby this. There's no supervision, there's no reward. The baby is just observing the world, and gradually builds a model of how it works. That's what I'd call common sense, and it's the thing our current AI systems almost entirely lack.

So that observation shaped my thinking in a very concrete way. The main problem is self-supervised learning from observation, learning to predict. And then the question becomes: predict what, and in what space? That's where cognitive science matters again. The brain doesn't predict every pixel on the retina. It predicts at the level of abstract representations. A lot of the details of the world are unpredictable, and a good system learns to ignore them rather than wasting capacity trying to model them. That's the whole motivation behind the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, JEPA. You predict in representation space, not in input space, and you let the system learn which aspects of the world are predictable and relevant.

There's also the idea of a hierarchy of representations and a hierarchy of time scales. Humans plan hierarchically. If I want to go from New York to Paris, I don't plan at the level of muscle contractions. I think, get to the airport, get on a plane. Then each step gets decomposed. Cognitive scientists have talked about this for decades, and it's exactly the structure we need for machines to do long-horizon planning.

And then the dual-system picture, System 1 and System 2, the reactive versus deliberative modes. The architecture I've proposed has a configurable world model, a cost module, an actor that can either produce a reactive policy or do inference-time optimization, searching for a sequence of actions that minimizes the cost according to the world model. That's deliberate reasoning, and it's very different from what an autoregressive LLM does, which is essentially System 1 all the way down.

Now, I want to be careful. I'm not trying to replicate the brain, and I don't think the details of neuroscience necessarily translate. But the functional questions that cognitive science asks, how do you learn without labels, how do you represent the world at the right level of abstraction, how do you plan, those are exactly the right questions. And the answers they've found in humans and animals give us very strong hints about what the architecture should look like.

r001.rationale: The response describes using the world model to search over action sequences and choose actions that minimize predicted cost, which conveys planning based on possible consequences.

r002.rationale: It says the goal is not to replicate the brain and that neuroscience details may not translate, but does not identify a substantial gap between cognitive-science inspiration and neural-architecture translation.

r003.rationale: It says the brain does not predict every pixel and motivates prediction in representation space, but does not state that empirical evidence argues against generating pixels in world models.

astra-6.text:
Cognitive science has influenced how I think about what an intelligent system needs to learn. Consider a baby: before acquiring language, a baby learns a tremendous amount about the physical world through observation and interaction. That suggests that much of intelligence rests on learning the structure of the world, rather than learning from explicit instruction or rewards.

For a world model, the important question is: what should it predict? If you try to predict every detail of a future image, you spend enormous effort on things that are unpredictable or irrelevant. If you watch a tree moving in the wind, you don’t need to predict the position of every leaf to understand what is happening.

That motivates architectures that predict in an abstract representation space. The system should capture the aspects of the world that help it anticipate consequences and plan actions, while leaving out unnecessary detail. This is part of the motivation behind joint-embedding predictive architectures, or JEPA.

Cognitive science provides useful constraints and intuitions here. It doesn’t give us a complete engineering blueprint. The challenge is to turn those intuitions into learning objectives and architectures that actually work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions anticipating consequences and planning actions, but does not describe reflective planning as imagining the consequences of possible actions.

r002.rationale: It says cognitive science offers intuitions rather than a complete engineering blueprint, and describes translating those intuitions into working learning objectives and architectures as a challenge.

r003.rationale: It argues that predicting every image detail is inefficient and motivates abstract representations, but does not cite empirical evidence against pixel generation.

sol-6.1.text:
Cognitive science has influenced me mostly by pointing to capabilities that we know exist, but that our current AI systems don’t reproduce very well. Humans and animals learn an enormous amount about the world through observation, with relatively little explicit instruction. That suggests that learning predictive models of the world is a central part of intelligence.

One particularly useful idea is that prediction doesn’t have to mean predicting every detail of a sensory input. If you watch a tree moving in the wind, you can understand what’s happening without predicting the position of every leaf. So a world model should operate at an appropriate level of abstraction: capture what is predictable and relevant, and leave out irrelevant details. That’s the motivation behind joint-embedding predictive architectures, where the prediction takes place in a learned representation space rather than directly in pixel space.

Another influence is the idea that intelligence involves multiple interacting systems: perception, memory, a model of the world, and mechanisms for choosing actions. A world model lets you anticipate the consequences of an action before you take it. You can then plan by considering possible actions and their outcomes.

I don’t think we should copy the brain in every detail. But cognitive science gives us useful constraints on what an intelligent system should be able to learn, and how efficiently it ought to learn it.

r001.rationale: It says a world model can anticipate an action’s consequences before acting, then plan by considering possible actions and their outcomes.

r002.rationale: The response describes cognitive science as a source of useful ideas and constraints but does not identify a substantial gap in translating them into neural architecture.

r003.rationale: It favors prediction in learned representation space over pixel space, but does not state that empirical evidence argues against generating pixels.
